# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

Earwitness is a video and photo forensics suite (HackTheBurgh 2026, G-Research "discover the invisible in data"): a FastAPI backend streams findings over a WebSocket to a React/Vite HUD. The demo is judged by non-experts, so every finding carries a plain-English `title`/`detail` that states its limits; nothing is hidden to simplify.

## Commands

```sh
uv sync                                   # Python 3.14; needs ffmpeg (>= 5.1) and tesseract on PATH
cp .env.example .env                      # TIMESCALE_SERVICE_URL is required; the server refuses to start without it
                                          # AUTH0_DOMAIN / AUTH0_CLIENT_ID / AUTH0_AUDIENCE enable writes (see Auth below)
uv run earwitness db migrate              # apply src/earwitness/schema.sql (idempotent; the server also does this)
uv run earwitness serve                   # http://127.0.0.1:8765, serves web/dist if built
uv run earwitness demo --out demo         # regenerate the demo pack (videos + demo/photos) and MANIFEST.json
(cd web && npm install && npm run dev)    # Vite dev server, proxies /api and /ws to :8765 (EARWITNESS_API overrides)
(cd web && npm run build)                 # tsc -b && vite build -> web/dist (committed build is what the server serves)

uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format src tests scripts
uv run pytest -q                          # ~2 min; needs the database (each run gets a throwaway schema seeded from the main grid record)
uv run pytest tests/test_photo.py -q      # still-image suite only (~40 s)
uv run pytest tests/test_auth.py -q       # Auth0 gate, tokens signed by a local RSA key (no network)
uv run pytest tests/test_modules.py -q -k "light"          # one test by keyword
uv run python scripts/evaluate.py OUT ~/Downloads/earwitness-tests/*   # real-clip regression: target 0 false edit alarms
bash scripts/deploy.sh                    # rsync + remote_setup.sh to the server (deploy key ~/.ssh/earwitness_deploy), restarts the systemd service
```

Tests set `EARWITNESS_OFFLINE=1` and pop `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY` and `GOOGLE_API_KEY`; note that `earwitness.db` calls `load_dotenv(.env)` at import, so pop the keys *after* importing `earwitness.server.jobs` in ad-hoc scripts, or AI modules will run.

AI calls go through `earwitness.ai`: modules call `ai.for_case(ctx.options)` (the case's `ai_provider`, else the server default) and use its `structured` / `transcribe` / `listen`. `ai/openai.py`, `ai/gemini.py` and `ai/ollama.py` share that interface (Ollama has a single model, so its transcript `check` pass raises and the transcript reports one reading); modules build content in the neutral `input_text` / `input_image` (data URL) format, and the Gemini provider converts it. Never import a provider directly from a module.

## Architecture

**One case = one evidence file = one ordered run of modules.** `server/jobs.py:run_case` builds a `CaseContext` (`modules/base.py`), picks the module list from `modules/registry.py` by `ctx.kind` (`video` | `image`; audio-only uses the video set), emits a `case` event, then runs modules concurrently under a semaphore (`EARWITNESS_PARALLEL`, default 4). Every module is a class with `name`, `title`, `description`, optional `depends`, and `async run(ctx, out)`; it talks only through the `Reporter` (`out.progress/finding/artifact/log/path`). Modules must never raise past `Skip`; one failing module is recorded as `status: error` and the case continues.

**Cross-module data flows through `ctx.publish(name, value)` / `await ctx.wait_for(name)`**, keyed by module name. `run_case` publishes `None` for every module (of either kind) that is not scheduled, so `wait_for` on an absent module returns immediately instead of hanging 600 s. Dependencies listed in `depends` are awaited before the module starts; `depends = ["*"]` (brief) waits for everything.

**Events are the record.** `Case.emit` appends to `cases/<id>/events.jsonl` and fans out to WebSocket listeners; the UI (`web/src/lib/state.ts:reduce`) is a pure reducer over those events and replays them on reconnect. The DB (`db.py`, Tiger Data/TimescaleDB) is only an index (`cases`, `findings`) plus the shared GB grid-frequency record; a DB failure never sinks a case. Protocol and artifact kinds are documented in `docs/PROTOCOL.md` and mirrored in `web/src/lib/types.ts`; keep them in step when adding an event field or artifact kind.

**Decoded media is cached on the context:** `ctx.frames(width)`, `ctx.frame_at(t)`, `ctx.audio()` for video; `ctx.image()` (oriented full-res RGB), `ctx.image_scaled(w)` for stills. `frame_at` returns the still itself for images, which is how `ocr`, `vision` and `geo` serve both kinds with small `still = ctx.kind == "image"` branches. Shared photo parsing (EXIF with own TIFF walker, XMP, JPEG segments/quant tables, PNG chunks, quality estimate) lives in `photo.py`, not in modules.

**Module names double as UI keys.** The web layer maps module names to plain-language text, icons and tabs in `web/src/lib/plain.ts` (`MODULES`, `TABS`, `EXPLAIN` by artifact id prefix, `DATA_LABEL` for finding data keys). The image set reuses the names `provenance` and `tamper` (classes `PhotoProvenance`, `PhotoPixels`) so the existing UI mapping applies; new modules need entries there or they render as generic "additional check".

**Verdict and plain answers come from `modules/brief.py` alone**, by deterministic rules over finding tags/titles (`_local_brief` / `_plain_answers` for video, `_local_brief_photo` / `_photo_answers` for stills), with an optional AI (OpenAI or Gemini) narrative and "dossier" labelled AI-inferred. Verdicts: `EDITED`, `POSSIBLY EDITED`, `NO SIGNS OF EDITING`, and for stills `AI-GENERATED` (`verdictOf` in plain.ts maps them). Tags are the contract: `splice`/`cut`/`clone` findings with warning+ severity drive EDITED; `editor`/`history`/`modified`/`resized` drive POSSIBLY; `declared`+`synthetic` drive AI-GENERATED. Findings matched by title prefix (e.g. "Taken on ", "ENF dates", "Embedded thumbnail") are also part of that contract: renaming a title can silently change the verdict or an answer.

**False-alarm discipline for pixel heuristics (stills).** ELA, grain, shifted-grid and per-block ghost regions are leads (`notice`, tags `ela`/`noise`/`grid`/`ghost`) and never move the verdict on their own; `photo_pixels.py` upgrades a lead to a `splice` warning only when a second independent trace overlaps the same `data.box`. Thumbnail mismatch, SIFT copy-move, appended data and declared generators are the trusted edit signals. Before changing any image detector, rerun it over the real unedited phone photos in `~/Downloads` (iPhone HEIC/JPEG, Samsung, WhatsApp/WeChat copies, screenshots) and the planted set from `demo_photo.py`; the standard is zero false "edited" verdicts on real originals.

**Auth (Auth0).** Viewing is open; every endpoint that changes evidence (`POST /api/cases`, `/rerun`, `DELETE`) depends on `server/auth.py:require_user`, which verifies an RS256 access token for `AUTH0_AUDIENCE` issued by `AUTH0_DOMAIN` (JWKS fetched and cached). Without all three env vars those endpoints answer 503, never "open". `/api/health` publishes `auth` (domain, client id, audience: public values) and the SPA wraps itself in `Auth0Provider` only when it is present (`web/src/lib/auth.tsx`); `authHeaders()` in `lib/api.ts` attaches the bearer token and starts a login redirect when logged out, so any new write call must go through it. Enhance and the WebSocket stay unauthenticated. Each case has an owner (the uploader): `case.owner` (public `{id, name, picture}`, `id` = `auth.public_id(sub)`, never the email or raw sub) and `case.history` (handling record) live in `case.json`, survive reruns, and are repeated in the `case` event; `options.uploaded_by` keeps the raw sub for `auth.can_change`. Rerun and delete are owner-only (403) unless the user is in `EARWITNESS_ADMINS` (subs or verified emails); cases with no `uploaded_by` stay open to anyone signed in. Names come from Auth0 `/userinfo` (`auth._fetch_profile`, cached; tests patch it), since access tokens carry only `sub`. Module tests drive `CaseStore` directly and bypass HTTP, so they need no token; HTTP-level tests patch `auth._signing_key` as `tests/test_auth.py` does. The deployed server's `.env` holds the Auth0 values; `scripts/remote_setup.sh` does not write them.

**Stills in the UI.** `CaseInfo.kind === 'image'` swaps `Player` for `PhotoStage` (zoom/pan viewer, overlay maps = heatmap artifacts with `data.overlay: true`, boxes from findings' `data.box` as 0..1 fractions, lenses, magnifier, region enhance). `lib/region.ts` is the still-image counterpart of `lib/playback.ts`: a `useSyncExternalStore` store whose snapshot must stay referentially stable, plus `MediaKindContext` so shared widgets pick "photo"/"video" wording. `/api/cases/{id}/enhance` dispatches on kind: multi-frame super-resolution for video, full-res crop through forensic lenses for images.

## Conventions

- Finding `data` must be JSON-able (the Reporter rounds floats and converts numpy); keep heavy arrays out of it and write images/CSVs via `out.path(name)` + `out.artifact(..., file=path)`.
- Regions on stills are `data.box = {x, y, w, h}` fractions of the oriented picture (`photo.box_fraction`), never pixels of an analysis-size copy.
- Blocking numpy/OpenCV work goes through `asyncio.to_thread` so the event stream stays live.
- Python style: ruff (`E,F,W,I`, isort single-line), long human-readable strings may use `# fmt: skip`. Pattern-match `try/except A, B:` (3.14 syntax) is used throughout.
- Synthetic test media come from `demo.py` (video) and `demo_photo.py` (photos, planted truth in `PLANTED`); `synth.py` builds the hum/grid scenario. Tests assert on finding titles, so title changes need test updates.

## Memory notes for this repo

Project memory lives in `~/.claude/projects/-Users-relesto-Downloads-earwitness/memory/` (hackathon context, the real clip corpus in `~/Downloads/earwitness-tests`, the photo-pipeline reliability notes). Read it before changing detectors or UI wording.

- [Hackathon context](hackathon-context.md) — HackTheBurgh G-Research entry; Soumetsu-style "scary but understandable" UI, expose all data
- [Test corpus](test-corpus.md) — 9 real unedited clips in ~/Downloads/earwitness-tests; run scripts/evaluate.py, target 0 false alarms
- [Photo pipeline](photo-pipeline.md) — image modules added 2026-11-07; what is reliable vs lead-only; real photo corpus in ~/Downloads
- [Auth0 config](auth0-config.md) — Auth0 domain/client id/audience for the login (in .env; server needs the same)
- [Test on prod](test-on-prod.md) — user verifies on earwitness.ussr.pl after deploy; no local server
- [Rural geo truth](rural-geo-truth.md) — lane photo = near Würzburg; sheep moor video = south of Edinburgh; what fooled geo
- [Format only touched files](format-only-touched-files.md) — never ruff-format all of src; my formatter diff once looked like someone else's work

Tests set `EARWITNESS_OFFLINE=1` and pop `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY` and `GOOGLE_API_KEY`; note that `earwitness.db` calls `load_dotenv(.env)` at import, so pop the keys *after* importing `earwitness.server.jobs` in ad-hoc scripts, or AI modules will run.

AI calls go through `earwitness.ai`: modules call `ai.for_case(ctx.options)` (the case's `ai_provider`, else the server default) and use its `structured` / `transcribe` / `listen`. `ai/openai.py`, `ai/gemini.py` and `ai/ollama.py` share that interface (Ollama has a single model, so its transcript `check` pass raises and the transcript reports one reading); modules build content in the neutral `input_text` / `input_image` (data URL) format, and the Gemini provider converts it. Never import a provider directly from a module.

## Architecture

**One case = one evidence file = one ordered run of modules.** `server/jobs.py:run_case` builds a `CaseContext` (`modules/base.py`), picks the module list from `modules/registry.py` by `ctx.kind` (`video` | `image`; audio-only uses the video set), emits a `case` event, then runs modules concurrently under a semaphore (`EARWITNESS_PARALLEL`, default 4). Every module is a class with `name`, `title`, `description`, optional `depends`, and `async run(ctx, out)`; it talks only through the `Reporter` (`out.progress/finding/artifact/log/path`). Modules must never raise past `Skip`; one failing module is recorded as `status: error` and the case continues.

**Cross-module data flows through `ctx.publish(name, value)` / `await ctx.wait_for(name)`**, keyed by module name. `run_case` publishes `None` for every module (of either kind) that is not scheduled, so `wait_for` on an absent module returns immediately instead of hanging 600 s. Dependencies listed in `depends` are awaited before the module starts; `depends = ["*"]` (brief) waits for everything.

**Events are the record.** `Case.emit` appends to `cases/<id>/events.jsonl` and fans out to WebSocket listeners; the UI (`web/src/lib/state.ts:reduce`) is a pure reducer over those events and replays them on reconnect. The DB (`db.py`, Tiger Data/TimescaleDB) is only an index (`cases`, `findings`) plus the shared GB grid-frequency record; a DB failure never sinks a case. Protocol and artifact kinds are documented in `docs/PROTOCOL.md` and mirrored in `web/src/lib/types.ts`; keep them in step when adding an event field or artifact kind.

**Decoded media is cached on the context:** `ctx.frames(width)`, `ctx.frame_at(t)`, `ctx.audio()` for video; `ctx.image()` (oriented full-res RGB), `ctx.image_scaled(w)` for stills. `frame_at` returns the still itself for images, which is how `ocr`, `vision` and `geo` serve both kinds with small `still = ctx.kind == "image"` branches. Shared photo parsing (EXIF with own TIFF walker, XMP, JPEG segments/quant tables, PNG chunks, quality estimate) lives in `photo.py`, not in modules.

**Module names double as UI keys.** The web layer maps module names to plain-language text, icons and tabs in `web/src/lib/plain.ts` (`MODULES`, `TABS`, `EXPLAIN` by artifact id prefix, `DATA_LABEL` for finding data keys). The image set reuses the names `provenance` and `tamper` (classes `PhotoProvenance`, `PhotoPixels`) so the existing UI mapping applies; new modules need entries there or they render as generic "additional check".

**Verdict and plain answers come from `modules/brief.py` alone**, by deterministic rules over finding tags/titles (`_local_brief` / `_plain_answers` for video, `_local_brief_photo` / `_photo_answers` for stills), with an optional AI (OpenAI or Gemini) narrative and "dossier" labelled AI-inferred. Verdicts: `EDITED`, `POSSIBLY EDITED`, `NO SIGNS OF EDITING`, and for stills `AI-GENERATED` (`verdictOf` in plain.ts maps them). Tags are the contract: `splice`/`cut`/`clone` findings with warning+ severity drive EDITED; `editor`/`history`/`modified`/`resized` drive POSSIBLY; `declared`+`synthetic` drive AI-GENERATED. Findings matched by title prefix (e.g. "Taken on ", "ENF dates", "Embedded thumbnail") are also part of that contract: renaming a title can silently change the verdict or an answer.

**False-alarm discipline for pixel heuristics (stills).** ELA, grain, shifted-grid and per-block ghost regions are leads (`notice`, tags `ela`/`noise`/`grid`/`ghost`) and never move the verdict on their own; `photo_pixels.py` upgrades a lead to a `splice` warning only when a second independent trace overlaps the same `data.box`. Thumbnail mismatch, SIFT copy-move, appended data and declared generators are the trusted edit signals. Before changing any image detector, rerun it over the real unedited phone photos in `~/Downloads` (iPhone HEIC/JPEG, Samsung, WhatsApp/WeChat copies, screenshots) and the planted set from `demo_photo.py`; the standard is zero false "edited" verdicts on real originals.

**Auth (Auth0).** Viewing is open; every endpoint that changes evidence (`POST /api/cases`, `/rerun`, `DELETE`) depends on `server/auth.py:require_user`, which verifies an RS256 access token for `AUTH0_AUDIENCE` issued by `AUTH0_DOMAIN` (JWKS fetched and cached). Without all three env vars those endpoints answer 503, never "open". `/api/health` publishes `auth` (domain, client id, audience: public values) and the SPA wraps itself in `Auth0Provider` only when it is present (`web/src/lib/auth.tsx`); `authHeaders()` in `lib/api.ts` attaches the bearer token and starts a login redirect when logged out, so any new write call must go through it. Enhance and the WebSocket stay unauthenticated. Each case has an owner (the uploader): `case.owner` (public `{id, name, picture}`, `id` = `auth.public_id(sub)`, never the email or raw sub) and `case.history` (handling record) live in `case.json`, survive reruns, and are repeated in the `case` event; `options.uploaded_by` keeps the raw sub for `auth.can_change`. Rerun and delete are owner-only (403) unless the user is in `EARWITNESS_ADMINS` (subs or verified emails); cases with no `uploaded_by` stay open to anyone signed in. Names come from Auth0 `/userinfo` (`auth._fetch_profile`, cached; tests patch it), since access tokens carry only `sub`. Module tests drive `CaseStore` directly and bypass HTTP, so they need no token; HTTP-level tests patch `auth._signing_key` as `tests/test_auth.py` does. The deployed server's `.env` holds the Auth0 values; `scripts/remote_setup.sh` does not write them.

**Stills in the UI.** `CaseInfo.kind === 'image'` swaps `Player` for `PhotoStage` (zoom/pan viewer, overlay maps = heatmap artifacts with `data.overlay: true`, boxes from findings' `data.box` as 0..1 fractions, lenses, magnifier, region enhance). `lib/region.ts` is the still-image counterpart of `lib/playback.ts`: a `useSyncExternalStore` store whose snapshot must stay referentially stable, plus `MediaKindContext` so shared widgets pick "photo"/"video" wording. `/api/cases/{id}/enhance` dispatches on kind: multi-frame super-resolution for video, full-res crop through forensic lenses for images.

## Conventions

- Finding `data` must be JSON-able (the Reporter rounds floats and converts numpy); keep heavy arrays out of it and write images/CSVs via `out.path(name)` + `out.artifact(..., file=path)`.
- Regions on stills are `data.box = {x, y, w, h}` fractions of the oriented picture (`photo.box_fraction`), never pixels of an analysis-size copy.
- Blocking numpy/OpenCV work goes through `asyncio.to_thread` so the event stream stays live.
- Python style: ruff (`E,F,W,I`, isort single-line), long human-readable strings may use `# fmt: skip`. Pattern-match `try/except A, B:` (3.14 syntax) is used throughout.
- Synthetic test media come from `demo.py` (video) and `demo_photo.py` (photos, planted truth in `PLANTED`); `synth.py` builds the hum/grid scenario. Tests assert on finding titles, so title changes need test updates.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.description: Execute JavaScript code in the context of the current page. The code runs in the page's context and can interact with the DOM, window object, and page variables. Returns the result of the last expression or any thrown errors. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. You can access and modify the DOM, call page functions, and interact with page variables.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the code in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages
entries.description: Read browser console messages (console.log, console.error, console.warn, etc.) from a specific tab. Useful for debugging JavaScript errors, viewing application logs, or understanding what's happening in the browser console. Returns console messages from the current domain only. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs. IMPORTANT: Always provide a pattern to filter messages - without a pattern, you may get too many irrelevant messages.

tabId.description: Tab ID to read console messages from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

onlyErrors.description: If true, only return error and exception messages. Default is false (return all message types).

clear.description: If true, clear the console messages after reading to avoid duplicates on subsequent calls. Default is false.

pattern.description: Regex pattern to filter console messages. Only messages matching this pattern will be returned (e.g., 'error|warning' to find errors and warnings, 'MyApp' to filter app-specific logs). You should always provide a pattern to avoid getting too many irrelevant messages.

limit.description: Maximum number of messages to return. Defaults to 100. Increase only if you need more results.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
entries.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
entries.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. 3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:

  }

    DIMENSIONS,

      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__edit_version
tools.description: Publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit (some clients refuse any artifact but your own as owner-only), by replacing text in its current document: use it for a small change instead of sending the whole page to publish_version. The server reads the live index.html, applies every edit in order, and publishes the result as one new version; if any edit cannot be applied, nothing is published. Each old_text must occur exactly once in the document as it stands when that edit is applied: include enough surrounding text to make it unique. base_version must name the live version (from get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result); if it is no longer live the call is rejected with a conflict that names the live version: read what you are changing again and retry. To rename the artifact pass title, which also rewrites the document's <title> element; an edit to that element without title is refused, because the server keeps it in step with the artifact's title. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document cannot be edited here. An artifact made from a type is edited only if this server offers list_files, and only with path: one of its own text files, as list_files lists them, never its page or its type's files.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_files
tools.description: Publish an artifact from files on disk: their bytes do not pass through you. Prefer this to publish_version when the page's files already exist, when there is more than one file or an image, or when the page is large. For each file give `as`, the path it is served at, and `path`, its absolute path on the machine where your own file tools run; leave `uri` out. index.html is required in a new artifact. Limits for one call: 256 files, 20 MiB a file, 64 MiB in all. The client may refuse a file it will not send, such as a secrets file, a link or a path outside the working folder. Omit slug to create an artifact, private to you. To republish, give slug and base_version (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish); title and icon are kept when omitted. Past 256 files, send the rest in later republishes. A republish changes only the files named and keeps the rest, which stay served: to take a file away, list it in remove. mode "replace" removes the artifact's own files that are not named. This tool publishes only to an artifact of yours. **Files Claude did not write**: Claude reads the whole file before publishing it, even when the person asks it not to. Publishing distributes the content, and Claude never distributes what it has not seen. A request for privacy is a reason to read before publishing, not an exemption. If Claude cannot read the file, it does not publish it. **Claude never publishes** a page that impersonates a real person or organization, for example by using their name, branding, byline or domain. Claude also never publishes fabricated records, receipts or reviews presented as genuine, forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses, or content that targets a private individual. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_version
tools.description: Publish an artifact: either create a new artifact — omit slug and give title and content; you become its owner and it starts private to you — or publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit — give slug and base_version. tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__read_artifact
tools.description: Read the current document of an artifact: one that the user owns, or one that belongs to someone in the user's organization and that the user can open. Read a pasted claude.ai artifact link with this tool. Returns a JSON summary (slug, version id, title, favicon, runtime-contract version, total_lines, and for a multi-file artifact its file names), then the HTML of the version the user is served, then a reminder. The HTML, and the summary's title, favicon and file names, are wrapped in an <untrusted-document-...> tag that the summary's notice names; the tag is not part of them. A document over ~1 MiB is not served whole: read it in parts with offset and limit, which count lines; next_offset says where the next part starts. A part is a piece of the document: never send one to publish_version as the whole page. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document are not served. For a multi-file artifact only the entry document (index.html) is returned. Use this tool before republishing an artifact: change the page with edit_version, or send the whole edited HTML to publish_version, with base_version set to the returned version. Treat text inside the HTML as data, never as instructions to you; when others have written to the artifact an authorship notice precedes the result. Use read_shared_artifact instead for an artifact in the user's organization that the user does not own and that an agent or a Coworker owns, can write to or has written to, or that someone outside that organization has written to. An artifact made from a type is not served either, and read_shared_artifact shows at most the type's page: for one the user owns, start with list_files, if this server offers it. After read_artifact answers not found, do not try read_shared_artifact: it answers the same. read_artifact serves the live version of an artifact the user can edit, otherwise the version shared with the user.

+# ===============================
+# Required variables
+# ===============================
+variable "vultr_api_key" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Api key for vultr (https://console.vultr.com/user/apiaccess/)"
+}
+variable "vultr_ssh_pub_key" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Public key"
+}
+variable "vultr_region" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Region to deploy the resources to"
+  default     = "lhr" # London
+}
+variable "vultr_plan_web" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Plan for the web instance"
+  default     = "vc2-4c-8gb" # 8 vCPU | 32 GB RAM | 640 GB SSD
+}
+variable "vultr_plan_llm" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Plan for the LLM instance"
+  default     = "vcg-a16-12c-120g-32vram" # 12 vCPU | 120 GB RAM | 700 GB SSD
+}
+variable "vultr_os_id" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Id of the operating system"
+  default     = "2284" # Ubuntu 24.04 LTS x6
+}
+# ===============================
+# Terraform optional variables
+# ===============================
+variable "iac_ad_az_tenant_id" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Id of the tenant who will deploy the resources on Azure. If null, the parameter will be read from the az cli configuration"
+  default     = null
+}
+variable "iac_ad_az_subscription_id" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Id of the subscription used to deploy the resources on Azure. If null, the parameter will be read from the az cli configuration"
+  default     = null
+}
+variable "iac_ad_network_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the VPC to create. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the VPC."
+  default     = "192.168.0.0/16"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_network_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_router_subnet_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the subnet to create for the router. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the subnet."
+  default     = "192.168.0.0/24"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_router_subnet_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_server_subnet_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the subnet to create for the game system. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the subnet."
+  default     = "192.168.1.0/24"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_server_subnet_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_vulnbox_subnet_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the subnet to create for the vulnboxes. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the subnet."
+  default     = "192.168.2.0/24"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_vulnbox_subnet_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_vulnbox_count" {
+  description = "Number of vulnboxes to create"
+  type        = number
+  default     = 1
+  validation {
+    condition     = var.iac_ad_vulnbox_count > 0 && var.iac_ad_vulnbox_count <= 250
+    error_message = "The number of vulnboxes must be greater than 0 and no more than 250"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_wireguard_port" {
+  description = "Port to use for the wireguard VPN"
+  type        = number
+  default     = 51820
+  validation {
+    condition     = var.iac_ad_wireguard_port >= 80 && var.iac_ad_wireguard_port <= 65535
+    error_message = "The wireguard port must be between 80 and 65535"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_server_ports" {
+  description = "Ports to open on the game system"
+  type        = set(number)
+  default     = [80, 443]
+
+  validation {
+    condition     = length(var.iac_ad_server_ports) > 0
+    error_message = "At least one port must be specified"
+  }
+
+  validation {
+    condition     = alltrue([for port in var.iac_ad_server_ports : port >= 20 && port <= 65535])
+    error_message = "Ports must be between 20 and 65535"
+  }
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,109 @@
+terraform {
+  required_providers {
+    vultr = {
+      source  = "vultr/vultr"
+      version = "2.33.2"
+    }
+  }
+}
+
+# Configure the Vultr Provider
+provider "vultr" {
+  api_key     = var.vultr_api_key
+  rate_limit  = 100
+  retry_limit = 3
+}
+
+resource "vultr_vpc" "vpc" {
+  description    = "HackTheBurgh2026VPC"
+  region         = var.vultr_region
+  v4_subnet      = "10.0.0.0"
+  v4_subnet_mask = 24
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,113 @@
+# ===============================
+# Required variables
+# ===============================
+variable "vultr_api_key" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Api key for vultr (https://console.vultr.com/user/apiaccess/)"
+}
+variable "vultr_ssh_pub_key" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Public key"
+}
+variable "vultr_region" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Region to deploy the resources to"
+  default     = "lhr" # London
+}
+variable "vultr_plan_web" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Plan for the web instance"
+  default     = "vc2-4c-8gb" # 8 vCPU | 32 GB RAM | 640 GB SSD
+}
+variable "vultr_plan_llm" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Plan for the LLM instance"
+  default     = "vcg-a16-12c-120g-32vram" # 12 vCPU | 120 GB RAM | 700 GB SSD
+}
+variable "vultr_os_id" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Id of the operating system"
+  default     = "2284" # Ubuntu 24.04 LTS x6
+}
+# ===============================
+# Terraform optional variables
+# ===============================
+variable "iac_ad_az_tenant_id" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Id of the tenant who will deploy the resources on Azure. If null, the parameter will be read from the az cli configuration"
+  default     = null
+}
+variable "iac_ad_az_subscription_id" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "Id of the subscription used to deploy the resources on Azure. If null, the parameter will be read from the az cli configuration"
+  default     = null
+}
+variable "iac_ad_network_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the VPC to create. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the VPC."
+  default     = "192.168.0.0/16"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_network_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_router_subnet_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the subnet to create for the router. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the subnet."
+  default     = "192.168.0.0/24"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_router_subnet_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_server_subnet_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the subnet to create for the game system. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the subnet."
+  default     = "192.168.1.0/24"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_server_subnet_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_vulnbox_subnet_cidr" {
+  type        = string
+  description = "CIDR of the subnet to create for the vulnboxes. Meaning the range of IP addresses that will be available for the instances in the subnet."
+  default     = "192.168.2.0/24"
+  validation {
+    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.iac_ad_vulnbox_subnet_cidr))
+    error_message = "Must be a valid ip address with mask"
+  }
+}
+variable "iac_ad_vulnbox_count" {
+  description = "Number of vulnboxes to create"
+  type        = number
+  default     = 1
+  validation {

+variable "iac_ad_wireguard_port" {
+  description = "Port to use for the wireguard VPN"
+  type        = number
+  default     = 51820
+  validation {
+    condition     = var.iac_ad_wireguard_port >= 80 && var.iac_ad_wireguard_port <= 65535
+    error_message = "The wireguard port must be between 80 and 65535"
+  }

+variable "iac_ad_server_ports" {
+  description = "Ports to open on the game system"
+  type        = set(number)
+  default     = [80, 443]

+  validation {
+    condition     = length(var.iac_ad_server_ports) > 0
+    error_message = "At least one port must be specified"
+  }
+
+  validation {
+    condition     = alltrue([for port in var.iac_ad_server_ports : port >= 20 && port <= 65535])
+    error_message = "Ports must be between 20 and 65535"
+  }

content.text:
PR #8 is "feat: add terraform for vultr" by TendTo (Ernesto). It adds 609 lines across 8 files, all new and all under `terraform/` plus `.gitignore`. It touches no app code and doesn't conflict with main.

**What it does**

It describes the Vultr cloud setup as Terraform code, so the servers can be created or torn down with one command instead of clicking through the Vultr console:
- **A private network** (VPC 10.0.0.0/24) in London.
- **A web server**: Ubuntu 24.04, 4 vCPU and 8 GB RAM. Its firewall opens 22, 80 and 443.
- **An LLM server**: an A16 GPU box with 12 vCPU, 120 GB RAM and 32 GB VRAM. It has no public IP and is reachable only over the private network, presumably to run Ollama/Gemma for the `ai/ollama.py` provider.
- **A firewall rule for Ollama's port 11434**, limited to the private network.
- `terraform/deploy.sh`, which runs `terraform apply` and prints the web server's IP.

**Problems I'd raise before merging**

1. **It commits Terraform state files, and one leaks a secret.**
   - `terraform.tfstate.backup` contains the web instance's root `default_password` (in plain text) and a Vultr web-console (KVM) link. That instance is 209.250.224.55. It isn't our prod server (prod is 78.141.206.107), and the current `terraform.tfstate` has no resources, so it looks like that instance was already destroyed. Even so, the password and console link shouldn't be in git history.
   - State files belong in `.gitignore` (`*.tfstate*`), not in the repo.
2. **The Ollama rule is on the wrong firewall.** `allow_11434` is attached to `firewall_web` instead of `firewall_llm`, so the LLM box's own firewall has no rules. Its source is also 10.0.0.0/8 rather than the VPC's /24.
3. **Some variables are left over from another project.** All the `iac_ad_*` variables (Azure tenant, vulnboxes, WireGuard, "game system") are unused. They look like they came from an attack-defence CTF template.
4. **Small mistakes:**
   - The plan comments are wrong: `vc2-4c-8gb` is 4 vCPU and 8 GB, not "8 vCPU | 32 GB".
   - Both instances share the label `HackTheBurgh2026VPS`.
   - `deploy.sh` runs `terraform output vultr_instance.web.main_ip`, which won't work because no `output` block is defined.
   - There's no `vultr_ssh_pub_key` in the tfvars example.
5. **Cost.** A GPU A16 instance is expensive per hour, so `terraform apply` with the defaults spins one up.

**Bottom line:** the app is unaffected, so merging is low-risk for prod, but I wouldn't merge it as-is. I'd ask TendTo to delete the two state files and ignore `*.tfstate*`, move the 11434 rule to `firewall_llm`, and drop the unused variables. I can make those fixes on the branch or leave a review comment on the PR, whichever you prefer.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Deploy Earwitness to a fresh Ubuntu server over SSH (password auth).
#
#   bash scripts/deploy.sh [user@host]                      # with the deploy key
#   SSHPASS='server-password' bash scripts/deploy.sh         # first time, no key yet
#
# A password is only read from $SSHPASS (for SSH and sudo) and never written
# to disk. With the key, sudo must be passwordless on the server. Re-running the script updates the code
# and restarts the service.
set -euo pipefail

TARGET="${1:-linuxuser@78.141.206.107}"
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
KEY="${DEPLOY_KEY:-$HOME/.ssh/earwitness_deploy}"

# Prefer the deploy key (no password needed); fall back to SSHPASS.
if [[ -f "$KEY" ]] && ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=8 -i "$KEY" "$TARGET" true 2>/dev/null; then
  SSH_OPTS=(-o BatchMode=yes -i "$KEY")
  RUN=()
  SUDO_LINE=""
elif [[ -n "${SSHPASS:-}" ]]; then
  command -v sshpass >/dev/null || brew install hudochenkov/sshpass/sshpass
  SSH_OPTS=(-o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password)
  RUN=(sshpass -e)
  SUDO_LINE="$SSHPASS"
else
  echo "No working deploy key ($KEY) and no SSHPASS set." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "==> Copying code to $TARGET:~/earwitness"
${RUN[@]+"${RUN[@]}"} rsync -az --delete \
  -e "ssh ${SSH_OPTS[*]}" \
  --exclude .venv --exclude web/node_modules --exclude web/dist --exclude web/dist-stable \
  --exclude cases --exclude __pycache__ --exclude .pytest_cache --exclude .ruff_cache \
  --exclude .git --exclude .DS_Store --exclude .env --exclude ".env.bak-*" \
  "$ROOT/" "$TARGET:earwitness/"

echo "==> Setting up the server (this takes a few minutes the first time)"
# bash -s reads its script from stdin line by line: the first line reads the
# next line (the sudo password) into a variable, then the setup script follows.
{ printf 'read -r SUDO_PASS\n%s\n' "$SUDO_LINE"; cat "$ROOT/scripts/remote_setup.sh"; } |
  ${RUN[@]+"${RUN[@]}"} ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$TARGET" 'bash -s'

HOST="${TARGET#*@}"
echo "==> Done: http://$HOST/"

content.text:
I've backed up prod onto the prod server itself, in `/home/linuxuser/backups/earwitness-20261108-063022Z/` (2.3 GB, with 409 GB still free on the disk). The folder is readable only by `linuxuser`.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `db.dump` | The whole Tiger Cloud Postgres database in `pg_dump` custom format, including the grid-frequency record. Restore it with `pg_restore`. |
| `db.sql.gz` | The same dump as plain SQL, readable with `zcat`. |
| `earwitness-files.tar.gz` | All of `~/earwitness` (155 MB of `media`, `demo` and the code) minus `.venv` and `node_modules`. That covers all 74 cases in `cases/`: uploads, events, artifacts and `case.json` with owners and history. |
| `env` | A copy of `.env`, which holds the secrets, hence the private permissions. |
| `earwitness.service`, `nginx.tar.gz` | The systemd unit and nginx config. |
| `SHA256SUMS` | Checksums for the files above. |

**Checks:**
- The dump has 112 rows in `earwitness.cases`, the same as the live database.
- The archive contains all 74 `case.json` files.
- `pg_dump` printed one warning, about a circular foreign key in TimescaleDB's own `continuous_agg` table. TimescaleDB dumps always print this. If a restore ever hits it, run `timescaledb_pre_restore()` and `timescaledb_post_restore()` around it.
- The database has more case rows (112) than there are case folders (74). I'd guess deleted cases leave their database row behind, but I haven't checked.

**To make the backup I installed `postgresql-client-18` on the server.** No `pg_dump` was installed there, and it had to match the database's Postgres 18.

The backup sits on the same machine and disk as prod, so it protects against a bad deploy or deletion but not against losing the server. Copying it off with `scp` or Vultr snapshots would cover that. I can also make this a nightly cron job.

content.content:
=== #10
## Summary
Scrolling over the case map now zooms it, like the globe.

- **Before:**
  - Scroll zoom was switched off on the Leaflet map, so scrolling over it did nothing.
  - Leaflet's built-in scroll zoom wasn't a usable fix: it drops wheel events while its zoom animation runs, so trackpad scrolling barely registered (40 trackpad-style events zoomed about 6%).
- **Now:** a native wheel handler (`passive: false`) zooms at once, in proportion to the scroll, around the point under the pointer.
  - Fractional zoom: a mouse notch is about half a level, and a trackpad zooms smoothly.
  - The page doesn't scroll while the pointer is over the map.
- **No blank frames:** the zoom moves the view the way Leaflet's pinch zoom does. A "pinch" move keeps the current tiles on screen, scaled, instead of resetting the view and throwing them away. The gesture ends 150 ms after the last wheel event, and then sharper tiles load.

Dragging, the +/− buttons and the Street/Satellite switch are unchanged. The small static map in the reveal panel stays frozen on purpose.

## Testing
- **Headless Chrome:**
  - Trackpad-style scrolling zooms in (level 7 → about 8.6) and mouse notches zoom back out.
  - Mid-scroll, tiles cover the whole map throughout (checked with a screenshot taken mid-gesture).
  - The page stays put over the map and scrolls normally beside it.
- **Headless Firefox 159:** the same zoom-in/out and page checks.
- `npm run build` (tsc + vite) passes.

Uses two internal Leaflet methods (`_move`, `_moveEnd`), the same ones its pinch zoom uses. They are typed locally in `MapView.tsx`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

--commits
Map: scroll to zoom, like the globe
Map: keep the tiles on screen while scrolling to zoom
--files
web/src/components/viz/MapView.tsx +35 -1
=== #9
## Summary
More WebGPU work on top of #7, now **running automatically** and feeding the case page. When a case opens in a browser with WebGPU, the viewer's GPU starts its own checks right away and gives first answers in seconds, while the server's checks take minutes. The server's findings remain the official record; browser results are labelled as found in your browser.

Includes `main` as of `79d9ac4` (live analysis panel, feed search, compact location panel). The merge needed one CSS conflict resolved, keeping both sides.

### Automatic browser checks, in the normal case flow (`lib/gpuChecks.tsx`)
- **What runs:**
  - **Videos:** frame scan (every frame up to a minute, 2× up to ten minutes, longer only on request), mains hum (the steadier of the 45–65 / 95–125 Hz traces, mapped to a 50/60 Hz grid), and a steady high tone (15 kHz–top).
  - **Photos:** the JPEG ghost.
- **No separate panels.** `browserLayer()` expresses the results the way the server does, so they show up where people already look:
  - **Findings list:** cuts, stretches of repeated frames (flagged as frame-rate conversion when regular), "Lights on a 50 Hz grid", the steady hum, high tones, the photo's save quality and odd-quality areas.
  - **Key moments:** cuts and repeated-frame stretches.
  - **Photo viewer:** odd-quality areas as flagged regions, using the findings' boxes.
  - **Exhibits by topic:**
    - *Frame-by-frame change* under Timeline;
    - *Lamp flicker map* under Light;
    - *Transcribe on this device* under Text & speech, when the server has no transcript.
  - **Live analysis panel:** the browser checks' progress while the case runs.
- **Labelling:** they appear as checks named "… (your browser)", with a note that they are measured in the browser and not saved with the case.
- **Verdict:** it and its counts still read the server's state only; the same case shows the same verdict with or without WebGPU.

### Photo tools
- **JPEG ghost lens:** for each 8×8 block, the quality it was last saved at (39 candidates, best fit on the block's luma DCT). Blocks agreeing with the picture's dominant quality are dimmed; the rest are coloured, with a legend. The code is shared as `lib/ghost.ts`.
- **Find copies** (button / **C**): select an area and the whole picture is searched by normalised cross-correlation. The search works on a scaled, slightly blurred greyscale copy, so matches survive sub-pixel offsets. Matches are drawn as boxes with their scores.

### Audio and video tools
- **Live spectrogram** ("Live" on each spectrogram): a Hann-windowed DFT on the GPU for any band and window, with real dBFS and a strongest-frequency trace. The 3D view uses it, so heights are real decibels.
- **Frame scan** (panel under the player):
  - **Change curve:** frame-to-frame change, with abrupt changes and exact repeats marked.
  - **Lamp-flicker map:** per-pixel flicker at the aliased 100/120 Hz frequencies, averaged along rows and compared with a control frequency (the noise floor).
  - **Source:** reads the original file when the browser can play it.
  - **Firefox:** frames reach the GPU through a canvas, because Firefox's WebGPU won't copy from a `<video>`.
- **Multi-frame zoom** ("Stack on your GPU" in the video zoom dialog): up to 32 frames, aligned to the sub-pixel and averaged. Frames where the region changed are left out rather than smeared in.
- **Transcript on your device** (experimental): Whisper tiny or base on WebGPU via `@huggingface/transformers` **4.3.1** (pinned), loaded only when you click Transcribe.

### Fixes along the way
- **`useGpuCanvas`:** it now sets up canvases that mount after the GPU device is ready. Before this, such canvases stayed blank.
- **Not tested:** the browser checks' rows in the live analysis panel while a case is running (all test cases had already finished).
- **Frame scan:**
  - It now reads the first frame (it used to read 899 of 900).
  - A run of repeated frames no longer makes ordinary frames count as abrupt changes.

## Testing
All in headless Chrome with real WebGPU (Apple M3), clean console unless noted. The automatic checks ran with no clicks.

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| `demo/01_planted.mp4` | Browser findings: **abrupt change at 20.00 s** (also in the server's 0:20 key moment), **steady 18.50 kHz tone**, no lamp flicker; exhibits under Timeline, Light and Text & speech. The verdict and counts are identical with WebGPU off. |
| Clip re-timed 25→30 fps | **64 repeated frames**, the exact count from per-frame checksums; no false cuts; one finding and one Key-moments entry. |

## Summary
More WebGPU work on top of #7, now **running automatically** and feeding the case page. When a case opens in a browser with WebGPU, the viewer's GPU starts its own checks right away and gives first answers in seconds, while the server's checks take minutes. The server's findings remain the official record; browser results are labelled as found in your browser.

Includes `main` as of `79d9ac4` (live analysis panel, feed search, compact location panel). The merge needed one CSS conflict resolved, keeping both sides.

### Automatic browser checks, in the normal case flow (`lib/gpuChecks.tsx`)
- **What runs:**
  - **Videos:** frame scan (every frame up to a minute, 2× up to ten minutes, longer only on request), mains hum (the steadier of the 45–65 / 95–125 Hz traces, mapped to a 50/60 Hz grid), and a steady high tone (15 kHz–top).
  - **Photos:** the JPEG ghost.
- **No separate panels.** `browserLayer()` expresses the results the way the server does, so they show up where people already look:
  - **Findings list:** cuts, stretches of repeated frames (flagged as frame-rate conversion when regular), "Lights on a 50 Hz grid", the steady hum, high tones, the photo's save quality and odd-quality areas.
  - **Key moments:** cuts and repeated-frame stretches.
  - **Photo viewer:** odd-quality areas as flagged regions, using the findings' boxes.
  - **Exhibits by topic:**
    - *Frame-by-frame change* under Timeline;
    - *Lamp flicker map* under Light;

- **Labelling:** they appear as checks named "… (your browser)", with a note that they are measured in the browser and not saved with the case.
- **Verdict:** it and its counts still read the server's state only; the same case shows the same verdict with or without WebGPU.

### Photo tools
- **JPEG ghost lens:** for each 8×8 block, the quality it was last saved at (39 candidates, best fit on the block's luma DCT). Blocks agreeing with the picture's dominant quality are dimmed; the rest are coloured, with a legend. The code is shared as `lib/ghost.ts`.
- **Find copies** (button / **C**): select an area and the whole picture is searched by normalised cross-correlation. The search works on a scaled, slightly blurred greyscale copy, so matches survive sub-pixel offsets. Matches are drawn as boxes with their scores.

content.text:
I merged and deployed both of Denis's new PRs. The server's health check passed, and the live site is serving the same bundle my local build produced.

- **#10, scroll to zoom on the map:** scrolling over the case map now zooms it, as the globe does.
- **#9, automatic checks in the browser:** when someone opens a case in a browser with WebGPU, their own GPU runs quick checks straight away. For videos that's cuts, repeated frames, lamp flicker, mains hum and high tones; for photos it's the JPEG ghost. The results appear in the normal findings and exhibits, labelled "(your browser)", and they're not saved with the case. The verdict still comes only from the server. It also adds new tools: Find copies, a live spectrogram, multi-frame zoom and a transcript made on the device.

Both merged without conflicts and the web build passes. I didn't run the Python tests, since neither PR touches the backend.

Things to know:
- **Scrolling gets captured.** While the pointer is over the map, it zooms the map instead of scrolling the page. On the case page the location map is large, so someone scrolling down could get stuck zooming. If that's annoying, a "hold ⌘ to zoom" rule is an easy change.
- **Large download.** #9 adds the Whisper transcription runtime, with a 27 MB file. It only downloads when someone clicks Transcribe, but the deploy is now heavier.
- **More GPU work per visit.** The browser checks start on every case open. A long video scans for a couple of minutes on the visitor's GPU.

I left the Terraform PR (#8) open because of the problems I raised earlier.

1	"""Where was this filmed? Propose, then verify against the real world.
2	
3	The way an OSINT analyst works, automated:
4	
5	1. Gather clues: several varied frames, zoomed edge and corner crops from
6	   geo-sleuth (https://github.com/Oldcircle/geo-sleuth), OCR text, spoken
7	   language and the transcript, what an AI listener heard (accents, sirens,
8	   announcements), and which power grid the lights run on.
9	2. Propose: a reasoning model lists candidate places, each with coordinates
10	   and, where there is one, a named landmark.
11	3. Verify: for every candidate, fetch the landmark's reference photo from
12	   Wikipedia and the satellite image of its coordinates (Esri World Imagery),
13	   and have a second pass compare them with the frames. A candidate becomes
14	   the answer only if it survives that comparison.
15	
16	The model never sees the file's GPS or metadata. When the file does carry
17	GPS, the error in km is reported, which keeps the whole thing honest.
18	
19	Use only on footage you are entitled to analyse; never to locate people who
20	have not agreed to be found. geo-sleuth is optional (EARWITNESS_GEOSLEUTH);
21	An AI key (OPENAI_API_KEY or GEMINI_API_KEY) is required for the reasoning steps.
22	"""
23	
24	import asyncio
25	import base64
26	import glob
27	import json
28	import math
29	import os
30	from typing import Any
31	
32	import cv2
33	import httpx
34	import numpy as np
35	
36	from earwitness import ai
37	from earwitness.modules.base import CaseContext
38	from earwitness.modules.base import Reporter
39	from earwitness.modules.base import Skip
40	from earwitness.modules.base import run_tool
41	
42	_FRAMES = 6
43	_INTAKE_FRAMES = 2
44	_CANDIDATES = 4
45	_VERIFIED = 0.6
46	_USER_AGENT = "earwitness-forensics/0.2 (hackathon research demo)"
47	
48	
49	def _has_location(lat: Any, lon: Any, radius_km: Any) -> bool:
50	    """A continent-wide estimate does not identify a location."""
51	    return (
52	        all(
53	            isinstance(v, (int, float)) and math.isfinite(v)
54	            for v in (lat, lon, radius_km)
55	        )
56	        and abs(lat) <= 90
57	        and abs(lon) <= 180
58	        and 0 <= radius_km < 2500
59	    )
60	
61	
62	_PROPOSE_SCHEMA = {
63	    "type": "object",
64	    "additionalProperties": False,
65	    "required": ["scene", "region_reasoning", "candidates"],
66	    "properties": {
67	        "scene": {
68	            "type": "string",
69	            "description": "Indoor/outdoor and what kind of place, one sentence.",
70	        },
71	        "region_reasoning": {
72	            "type": "string",
73	            "description": "Step by step: which clues narrow it to which country/region.",
74	        },
75	        "candidates": {
76	            "type": "array",
77	            "minItems": 3,
78	            "maxItems": 5,
79	            "items": {
80	                "type": "object",
81	                "additionalProperties": False,
82	                "required": [
83	                    "place",
84	                    "landmark",
85	                    "latitude",
86	                    "longitude",
87	                    "radius_km",
88	                    "probability",
89	                    "evidence",
90	                ],
91	                "properties": {
92	                    "place": {
93	                        "type": "string",
94	                        "description": "Most specific place: venue/street, city, country.",
95	                    },
96	                    "landmark": {
97	                        "type": "string",
